Customs Inquiry Committee
On the Orders of the Day:

I would like to ask the leader of the government by what rule of procedure of parliament the government was authorized to retain two eminent counsel, Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C. and Mr. Eugene Lafleur, K.C., presumably, as reported by the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) this morning to the committee of inquiry into customs matters, for the purpose of representing that committee. The retaining of these counsel preceded the organization meeting of the committee and was done without consultation of the committee. These two eminent counsel have been brought to Ottawa, and when the committee met this morning it was instructed that counsel had been retained for the committee by the government. By what rule of parliamentary procedure is the government authorized on any occasion, and particularly on this occasion, to retain counsel for a committee prior to its organization and without consulting it?
Hon. GEORGE H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise:	If the question asked
by my hon. friend and the long argument which accompanied it are perfectly in order, the matter having been already discussed in committee this morning, and one of the rules of the House, if I understand them correctly, providing that any matter under consideration by a committee is not debatable upon the floor of the House, I will give the hon. member an answer. Only one counsel has so far been engaged by the government. On Sunday evening I communicated with both Mr. Geoffrion and Mr. Lafleur to ascertain if either would be available. Mr. Eugene Lafleur was not sure that he would be able to act and he has not been engaged. The services of Mr. Aime Geoffrion were retained, and the government offered to the committee this morning that he would be secured to assist the committee if the committee so desired. One member of the committee- I will leave the House to judge who that hon. member was-objected very strenuously to his engagement as counsel for the committee. The committee agreed however to recognize him as attorney for the Department of Customs and Excise, for the purpose, not of defending the department but Of probing into the administration of the department, correcting any irregularities that may be found and protecting the customs and excise revenue of Canada.
Mr. Speaker-

I have allowed the question of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and the answer of the Minister of Customs and Excise, because I consider this a matter of public importance and tantamount to a ministerial declaration. But I will remind hon. members that until a committee reports, it is irregular to refer to its proceedings in debate in the House. Paragraph 2*14, page 67 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, states:
For instance, in the session of 1873, Mr. Huntingdon-
Who 'became Postmaster General later on. -was proceeding to refer .to certain papers and letters relative to an important matter under the consideration of a select committee, but the speaker decided in accordance with English precedents that they could not be read in the House.
It is the practice that until a report is made to the House by a. special committee or any other committee, matters discussed before such committee cannot be debated in the House.
The question did not appertain to the proceedings before the committee, but to proceedings which took place before the committee was organized.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was discussed in committee this morning.

The query was in order as was also the answer, which I regarded as a ministerial declaration. But surely no one will deny that, in the absence of a report to the House of the special committee, the proceedings of that committee may not be debated here.
Ml1. STEVENS: I gather from your ruling, Mr. Speaker, that I have not transgressed the rules of the House in putting the question.

No; as I have said, I regarded both the query and the answer as being perfectly in order. The answer in my opinion wias a ministerial declaration upon a question which was perfectly allowable on the orders of the day.

The House resumed from Monday, February 8 consideration of the motion of Mr. J. C. Elliott for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Sutherland (South Oxford).

Mr. Speaker, last night wdien the House adjourned I was endeavouring to show why little reliance can be placed upon the pledges of Liberal politicians when they are contesting elections. We find that in 1896 when the Liberal party came into power it disregarded many of the pledges on the strength of which it had won the elections. The same thing happened after their return to office in 1921. Now we are face to face with their latest pledges, but what these are worth it is difficult. to estimate. The government is very indefinite in regard to its fiscal policy, and in view of its post election record in 1896 and in 1921 we can only imagine just what course of action will be followed. The Speech from the Throne is so vague and1 so indefinite that it really gives us very little information. Unfortunately this state of affairs makes for instability in the business world of the Dominion, and the condition is likely to become more and more acute while the uncertainty continues. Naturally business people will not invest their money in expanding present industries or establishing new ones while this state of affairs lasts, and it is becoming very detrimental to our national welfare. Only yesterday I was talking with a commercial man representing a house which manufactures a particular line of goods and imports other lines from France and England. If there was any stability in the tariff, indeed if there was any guarantee that even the present protection would be continued, that concern is ready to establish factories here to manufacture those imported lines. That is just a sample of the disadvantages that the country is labouring under, and it is one of the reasons why at the present

850	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
time Canada is not enjoying the prosperity which it should enjoy.
No one can have failed to notice the drastic changes in policy enunciated in the Speech from the Throne from the policy set forth by the Prime Minister at Richmond Hill only a few months ago. Those two policies are so widely different that there is scarcely any similarity whatever between them. In face of the changes which the government has shown it is prepared to make in the short period of a few months in respect to vital national questions, it is impossible for business people to have any confidence in the stability of the administration or in the permanency of the tariff, and consequently the whole country is suffering. If a board of directors, elected at the annual meeting of a corporation, turned right about face on the policy they had been entrusted to carry out, immediately the shareholders would bring them sharply to account. Yet this government went to the polls last autumn with certain very definite pledges, and inside three or four months it presents to parliament a Speech from the Throne outlining policies entirely different from the pledges given to the electorate.
May I say a word to our Progressive friends? I have been speaking to some of them casually and I gather that they are very strongly in favour of the group system. I believe that as a rule they are thoroughly honest in their belief that this system is much better than the two-party system. But when we survey the field it is very difficult to see how a group system can work successfully in this country. It might be possible in a small, compact country for a number of groups to function fairly well as a government, but for such a vast area as Canada and with so many diverse viewpoints and so many varying sectional needs, one group here and other groups there will never be able to get together and reconcile their viewpoints so as to secure a majority in the House. What Canada needs is what it has had in the past-two large parties containing representatives from every part of the Dominion. Each party having among its members representatives from the Atlantic to the Pacific can consider the problems facing the country and treat them from a national instead of a merely sectional viewpoint. Only in that way will the great problems confronting this country get proper consideration, and only in that way will each section find its local ..needs attended to in a way consistent with the national welfare. Mr. Crerar recognized that last year after his retirement

from politics, when he pointed out how the Progressive party in parliament had failed in that regard. While I believe, as I say, that our Progressive friends are sincere in their convictions, I am sure they are making a very serious mistake, and I think that ultimately they will realize that these sectional groups cannot be of any real value in our political life. The group idea, especially as we have it here, is sectional, and its views are sectional. That is perfectly natural, in fact it could scarcely be otherwise. One of the reasons why we have heard in this House charges of bids, of auctioning, and so on, is that this group has not come out fairly and squarely at any time and told the House what it proposes to do under present conditions. In 1923 when the general election in Great Britain resulted in a return of a majority against the Conservative government, although the Conservatives were still the largest party in the House, Mr. Asquith, speaking as head of the smallest group, announced that his party would support the Labour party to form a government. That settled the whole difficulty. These gentlemen have never yet stated that they would support either one party or the other in office. I submit that that is not a fair position for them to take, for undoubtedly it adds to the uncertainty of the parliamentary situation, and I think in fairness to the country and in justice to both historic parties they should come out and declare unequivocally just where they stand. That "would at once obviate any charges of bids, purchasing and so forth, which are very detrimental to the dignity and honour of our parliamentary life.
The question of Maritime rights has been dealt with already, and I do not wish to discuss it at any length.
Would the hon. gentleman state that the Maritime lighters are not a sectional group?

In answer
to my hon. friend I may say that the Maritime righters, if you call them such, are squarely behind and have announced themselves as squarely behind the right hon. leader of the opposition.

I may inform the hon.
gentleman that there is a member on the opposite side of the House elected as a Maritime righter.

That is a
statement or an opinion of the hon. gentleman which I am not called upon to answer. The

point I wish to make is that with such uncertainty prevailing, the country has a right to know where every man and every group /stands in this regard. We have a group of Maritime province representatives who have been more or less organized along that line. I do not intend, however, to dwell on the question, because it has been fairly well dealt with and we will have an opportunity of discussing it later. I should like to put forward this view; the question of Maritime rights has been before the public for a number of years. Last year, during the election, Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King was in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; these matters were brought before him, and they have been brought before parliament and the government on many occasions during the past few years. Now, what are we offered in connection with these rights? What is our position in connection with our claims, as compared with the position of the Progressives with regard to their claims? Suppose that in the Speech from the Throne the Progressive group of to-day were offered a royal commission to deal with their claims, instead of having the promises already made in the Speech from the Throne, what would their answer be? I venture to say that the government would not be a government to-day. that that group would not accept the proposal for a royal commission and would have thrown the government out of power before this. There is hardly a question about that. I do not think the hon. member would deny it.
I wish to confirm that; }t is quite correct.

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
eepted, whose pledge is regarded as being as good as his bond; a man who will at all events make an honest, earnest attempt to carry out the policies of his party and' any pledges he may make. We have on the other hand the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, a man with ability, it is true, but a man who to-day has put himself, in the eyes of the country and I believe in the eyes of hon. members to some extent on both sides of the House, into the position of being a short-sighted opportunist who is willing, for the sake of remaining in power for a shorter or longer period, to jeopardize the future of his country for a generation to come. Which of these men are we going to entrust with the leadership of the government? The country to-day is ready to trust the man whom even the Progressives, while not supporting him, say they would rather trust than the man whom, while they say they have no confidence in him at all, they support. They know that in the leader of the opposition they have a man of great ability, a man with a clear, logical mind and a belief in the policies of his party and' in his own professions.
I feel that I have taken up more of the time of the House than a new member should, and I wish to express my appreciation to you, Sir, and to the members generally for the patience with which the House has listened to my remarks.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the House has been discussing now for a full month this important document, the Speech from the Throne, and the reply thereto, together with a number of other extraneous questions more or less associated with the Speech, and I think the country is beginning to wonder just how many more amendments our hon. friends opposite are going to make to it. Further, I think the opinion of the country is that it is about time we were proceeding with the work of the session.
Hear, hear.

One question upon *which the opposition and myself are agreed is that we should get down to business. Let us see what kind of business we have been engaged in so far, as a result of the obstructionist tactics of the opposition. We have had four amendments of various kinds put forward by the opposition. Two of them were direct amendments to the Address and the other two were more or less associated with it. Of the latter kind I refer to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) when we started out first, an amendment for which we have ever since been grateful to him. The other is the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I was going to say in the dead of night when other evils were abroad besides this kind of charge. That amendment has also been satisfactorily disposed of for the present at least. As regards the other two amendments, those made directly to the Address, the one moved by the leader of the opposition was of a somewhat insipid nature, capable of being construed in two or three ways, but it was also disposed of satisfactorily. This amendment was supposed to refer to the tariff. It spoke of employment or unemployment and of several other things, but the construction that could be put on it depended upon where you were speaking. One outstanding characteristic of the two amendments that were made to the Address was that neither of them proposed any change in the Speech from the Throne by way of eliminating anything. Am I to conclude from that that the leader of the opposition was agreeable to the Speech from the Throne provided that his little fiddle-de-dee amendment was added to it? Am I to conclude from the amendment moved yesterday by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) that he agreed with the Speech from the Throne provided that he could bring in some indefinite statement about some indefinite treaty that he did not mention? That is an extraordinary attitude to take towards a question of this nature.
Does my hon. friend not recognize the recent trade treaties entered into by the government?

But	my hon.
friend's whole speech, so far as I could gather, was against the Australian treaty, although it is not mentioned in the amendment at all.
The recent trade treaties.

Am I to conclude
that the speech was to be kept separate and these amendments to be used separately according to the exigencies of the occasion? Let any hon. member or any elector read this amendment alone and I ask:	Would he suppose it to be an attack upon the Australian treaty? Let me read it:
We desire respectfully to express regret that resulting from the policy of and recent trade agreements made by the present government the dairy products industry of Canada is now being subjected to most unfair and

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
unwarrantable competition from other countries, and that the Speech from the Throne gives no indication of any remedial legislation which would remove the discrimination under which this industry suffers.
The plural is used, meaning several treaties. There are only two treaties that I know of that affect the dairy industry, and those are the Australian treaty and the treaty with the West Indies. As the latter has not yet been confirmed by this parliament, I presume it is not the one referred to. By the process of attrition we come to the conclusion that it is the Australian treaty that is referred to, particularly when we take the hon. member's speech into consideration in connection with the amendment.
Mr. ME'IGHEN:	What about the French
treaty?

I was not aware
that that affected the dairy industry very substantially.
Mr. ME'IGHEN: The hon. member is not aware that it raised the duty against us on condensed milk by fifty per cent?

The effect has been so infinitesimal that even with the aid of powerful X-rays the dairymen have not been able to discover it yet.
Mr. ME.IGHEN:	It killed the condensed
milk trade with France.
Mr. MOTHERWElLL:	That is too bad.
Coming to the amendment of the hon. member for South Oxford, am I right in assuming that the hon. member is attacking the Australian treaty?

My hon. friend has asked a question. An order in council was put through, I think, in September, 190.5, extending to New Zealand the same privileges as were extended to Australia. Consequently, the amendment embodies New Zealand, Australia and France. Those are three which I had in mind.

We will get down to what it means, but how is the man in the country to secure the proper interpretation of it? The remedial legislation spoken of in the last few lines of the amendment must, I presume, be in the nature of either amending or abrogating the treaty. The only way that I know of by which we can effect remedial legislation is to do one or other of these two things. In the Speech from the Throne my hon. friend expects this to appear. The preparation of the Speech from the Throne was begun in anticipation of parliament meeting on the 10th December. That means that the

original drafting was started in November. The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) apparently expects this government, to enter seriously into a treaty with a sister dominion and then, after having consummated that treaty, and after it has been two months in operation, to incorporate into the Speech from the Throne an undertaking to abrogate or at least to amend that treaty. Is that what my hon. friend wants?

These objections could not apply to the order ,m council which was passed extending to New Zealand the same privileges that are embodied in the Australian treaty. New Zealand is the country from which we are receiving goods in large quantities as mentioned by me.

There would have
been no need of an order in council if the .Australian treaty had not been passed. We come back to the one inescapable conclusion, and that is that the Australian treaty was what my hon. friend meant and had in mind.

And the order in
council.

Very well. Now
are we to be held up indefinitely merely because a certain order in council was passed? It amounts to obstruction and nothing else, Mr. Speaker.

Does the hon. member
.regard six weeks' adjournment as facilitating the business of the House?

The six weeks are
gradually dwindling and we are only putting in the time.
That is not a very satisfactory answer.
It is as appropriate an answer as can be given to the question my hon. friend has asked.

I
rise to a point of order. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has stated that the amendment I moved was an obstruction pure and simple. I consider that statement absolutely out of order and I would ask him to withdraw it.
I take it back. Perhaps I may put it this way, that my hon. friend's purpose was to facilitate the passing of the Speech from the Throne.

There is a point of order before the House..

The Address-Mr. Motherwell

I take it back. It
must be one thing or the other; if the amendment does not constitute an obstruction it must be intended to facilitate the business of the House. If, however, there is an intermediary category in which I can classify the amendment I am willing to put it there. So far we have repulsed these various attacks-
I designate them attacks although I do not know whether some of them are worthy of that description.

Order. Lest there be
some misapprehension about the point of order which has been raised by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland),
I will cite Bourinot at page 365:
The terms "blocking" or "obstruction" have been ruled not out of order.
Hear, hear.

Order. Please do not
applaud the rulings of the Speaker. The minister has of course withdrawn the expression, but it is just as well that the House should be clear on the point. The word complained of has been used frequently, and personally I was in some doubt as to its admissibility.
I have looked up Bourinot and, as I have just quoted, he states that in England and in Canada the terms blocking and obstruction are considered not out of order.

My hon. friend
may choose whichever alternative he prefers.
You have taken it back anyway.

I have taken it
back all right; I am quite agreeable to do anything this afternoon. Now, other things being equal, Canada should promote as far as possible inter-imperial trade not only with the United Kingdom but with sister dominions, and a better way of improving the dairy industry than is suggested in this amendment is, in my opinion, to improve the quality not only of our export butter but of all other butter, and as well to improve the productivity of our dairy cow. After all it is the unit, the cow, that is the largest determining factor in the success of the industry. Bearing in mind these two points, let me now turn to the question raised by my hon. friend from South Oxford in regard to the importation of cheese. I assume that the hon. gentleman had no desire to mislead the House yesterday but certainly he was misinformed on the question. He spoke in large figures about the number of pounds of cheese imported into Canada last year, mentioning some 10,000,000 pounds. He quoted
the weekly letter of the Department of Agriculture in which the assembling of our own cheese and any other cheese we have in Montreal is reported. Usually it deals with Canadian cheese, but some 6,000,000 pounds of cheese were imported by the Kraft people from Great Britain less than a year ago and that product was not entered in the customs returns as New Zealand cheese. It was brought in by the Kraft people from Great Britain to 'be re-exported as process cheese. The Kraft people did not require all this cheese and they sold some of it to the Ingersoll Packing Company in the town of Ingersoll, and some of it apparently, after having paid the duty in the usual way, found itself in the town of my hon. friend. That I presume is the cheese to which he has been referring. I wish to clear this question up and in order to do so I desire to read from a memorandum supplied me this morning by Dr. Ruddick, the Dairy Commissioner. He says:
During March, April and May 1925, the Kraft Mar-Laren Cheese Company, Montreal, found it impossible to secure supplies of mature Canadian cheese for their business of processing. They therefore sent an agent to London, England, who purchased some 80,000 boxes (approximately 6,400,000 pounds) of New Zealand cheese and shipped them to Montreal from London. These cheese appear in the Customs returns as having been imported from the United Kingdom. These cheese were all to be used for making Kraft cheese which was to be re-exported to Europe.
So that my hon. friend did not get his returns from the Customs department, which would indicate the direct shipments from New Zealand. He got his information from a weekly letter supplied by my own department compiling the accumulation of stocks of cheese in the Montreal market-not in the port of Montreal but in the market.
The figures I quoted yesterday were taken from a statement issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce and not from the letter of the Department of Agriculture.

It says the Department of Agriculture, but if my hon. friend wants to correct it he is at liberty to do so. To proceed:

While I admire these gentlemen for being conscientious in their stand and true to the cause they represent, I do not consider their principles or their stand as being in the general interest of the country for which we are here to legislate; nor are their views those of the people of the west. It is true they represent a group and a class, and in that representation we must admire them, but their policy is of such a nature that it cannot meet with my approval.
I am going to take up the time of the House for a few moments in giving a summary of how the people of the western provinces voted during the last election. In the election of October 29 we had three parties running in the west. It is true that some candidates assumed the name of "Liberal-Progressive, or "Farmer and Labour," and others ran under the designation of "Farmer." But the lines were pretty closely defined, and I am going to bring to the attention of the House the votes cast respectively in the four western provinces including the Yukon to show what the people of the western provinces think of the fiscal policy which we should have in Canada. In British Columbia 90,018 votes were cast for the Conservative candidates;
63,374 for the Liberals; and 765 for the Progressives. In the Yukon the Conservatives received 742 and the Liberals 508, while the Progressives got no votes. Now I come to Alberta, which is the most highly organized farmer province in Canada. That organization has been functioning for a period of about fifteen years and it is significant that as compared with a membership which a few years ago totalled some 30,000 there are today in that province in the farmers' organization only 13,000 members. The people are leaving it, believing honestly that the interests Of the farmers of that province can best be served and their purpose better realized if the affairs of the province are taken out of the hands of purely class representation. From that province we have in this House ten Progressive members, representing 50,574 voters; three Conservative members representing a vote of 51,11(1 and we also have three Liberals with 44,277. Many a time I have heard it argued by members of that organization that representation in parliament should be in proportion to population, and if that policy were ever put into force the Progressive representation in this House to-day would be differently constituted.
The actual representation in this House from that province is 9, 4 and 3, not 10, 3 and 3.

Well, 9, 4 and 3. While the Conservative total vote in that province was, as I have pointed out, 51,111 represented by three Conservative candidates, four Liberal representatives with a total vote of 44,277, we have nine Progressive members returned by a total vote of 50,574. In Saskatchewan the Conservatives polled a total vote of 49,821, the Liberals 82,283, and the Progressives 62,411. In Manitoba the Conservatives received 70,331, the Liberals 34,554 and the Progressives 46,057. In other words, the Conservative majority in the four western provinces, including the Yukon, over the Liberal vote, was 37,025, while the Conservative majority over the vote recorded in the interests of the Progressive candidates was 102,214. I draw the attention of the House to these facts to show that the Progressive group to my left does not reflect the desire of the western people as it should: be reflected.
Now, I have heard various things discussed during this debate in reference to some of the candidates who took part in the election, and I am going to read for the information of hon. members, to indicate that there was no doubt as to the attitude of the Conservative candidate in East Calgary, an editorial which

The Address-Mr. Danis

was published by my opponent, the owner of the Calgary Albertan who by the way lost his deposit. The editorial in question appeared on October 28, the day before the election. It reads:
In choosing a member the electors of East Calgary will decide in the main for two principal reasons-'the one has to do with the candidate as a representative and the other has to do with the policy he supports. Mr. Davis, the third candidate, is not a resident of the riding and has not in any way, or at any time associated himself with the riding of the city of Calgary or the rural part of this constituency. Mr. Davis says that he will follow his leader in his anti-western policy which includes the destruction of the Crowsnest pass agreement and extreme increases in the tariff. He will join up with the opponents of the government electorate in the Maritime provinces who are asking support of the policy of the east against the west; he will link up with Ontario high protectionists who call for an average tariff of sixty per cent, and if this is not high enough they will increase it.
In addition, Mr. Davis has an enlarged policy which means declaration of tariff war. If East Calgary wants wider markets and better trade relations with its nearest neighbors; wants to be represented in parliament by a tariff jingo, they know where to find him.
The only comment I have to make on that editorial is that the policy which I advocated in that election was the policy of the Conservative party. We always did and we do believe in protection, though not protection for industry in the narrow sense intended in this editorial. We believe in protection for all of the people of Canada whereby more stable and more beneficial results may accrue to the country as a whole.
In this connection I desire to spend a few minutes in discussing the Australian treaty. We had the pleasure this afternoon of hearing a splendid and "intelligent address'' by the Minister of Agriculture on this subject, which is one of no small importance. I want to tell the Minister of Agriculture and the House that in British Columbia, in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, and in all the provinces of this Dominion, we have an industry which is associated with the manufacturing of butter and cheese and which has devoted a lifetime to the promotion of dairying in Canada. Through the different associations in Canada request after request has come to the Minister of Agriculture for relief from the disadvantages of the Australian and New Zealand treaties. This is an issue of extreme importance and one that calls for the serious consideration of the House. Last night we were told by one of the ministers that one of the reasons why these treaties should not be opposed was the fact that Australia and New Zealand purchased their lumber in the district adjacent to Vancouver and took it there to manufacture the boxes for the shipment of the product. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is something of more

importance to be taken into consideration than an argument of that nature. Prior to the election to which I have just referred, the dairy interests of Alberta deemed it advisable to publish a statement, part of which I will read:
Australian butter knocks two cents off local cream price. Why Alberta fanner is hit explained by the creamery men. Cannot compete with Australian butter on Montreal and Vancouver markets at present cream prices, says:
Manager Tully of Campbell and Griffin-P. Pallesen's announcement confirms foregoing.
Cream prices paid to farmers of western Canada have been reduced since October 15, in Manitoba and Saskatchewan from 42 cents per pound for special cream to 39 and 37 cents per pound respectively.
Alberta prices were held at the high standard until Saturday morning, when dealers were forced to reduce their prices from 42 to 40 cents per pound for special cream.
These reductions were made imperative because Australian and New Zealand butter can be landed on the English market much cheaper than the Canadian product at this season of the year. Also, Manitoba and Saskatchewan are able to undersell Alberta farmers on the home market.
The following resolution was passed by the farmers of a province which the Minister of Agriculture referred to as a province that would never favour protection-by the dairy interests of Saskatchewan, the home of the minister himself. It is headed:
Expansion of markets and increase in production also effective in causing greater financial returns.
I must admit that last year throughout the Dominion the increased production and the increased price as a whole showed a decided improvement for Canadian dairy interests. But we must realize the fact that there were only two months of last year during which this treaty was operative, and that while there was no detriment to the industry during that time, the general opinion, is that there is great danger of the industry suffering severely this year. At the convention it was stated in part:
Your directors further feel that it is their duty to draw to your attention the impending peril to the dairy interests of western Canada created by the Australian Trade Treaty passed near the close of the last session of the Dominion parliament, and which came into effect on October 1 of last year. This treaty reduces the duty on Australian butter entering Canada to 1 cent per pound, and permits the entry of Australian cheese duty free.
This tariff unfortunately is much lower than the British preferential tariff, and has already created a competition in Canada against Canadian dairy products which is destined to have a disastrous effect upon the dairy industry of Canada.
By virtue of a previous trade agreement with New Zealand, these Australian tariff rates likewise become automatically operative as far as New Zealand in concerned.
The Western Canada Dairy Association is formulating plans to resist the continuance of this trade agreement, and a delegation from this body will wait upon the Dominion government shortly to urge for the repeal
FEBRUARY 9, 1926	S67
The Address-Mr. Davis
of this portion of the treaty referred to. Our company will be represented on the delegation.
Following that I have a quotation from the Dairymen's Association of Ontario, referred to by the Minister of Agriculture, which association some time ago drafted a letter protesting against the Australian treaty, to which letter up to the time of this publication they had received no reply. They not only saw fit to give publicity to their communication with the department, that communication having been ignored, but also to write to several outstanding public men who might bring the matter before parliament.
For the benefit of the House I wish to read1 a letter from one of the largest creamery manufacturers in Alberta. If hon. members knew him as well as I do they would have no doubt whatever as to the correctness of his opinion with respect to the introduction of this treaty.

Does the
hon. gentleman refer to Mr. Pat Burns?

I have not yet mentioned
the name of anyone, but in reading this letter I am pleased to give the name of P. Bums and Company. They write:
Replying to your letter of November 7, asking for information with regard to the probable effect of the Australian Treaty, if you will secure a copy of the Calgary Herald of October 26, you will find therein an article under the heading, "Australian butter knocked two cents off local creamery price." This article is prepared by us and gives all the facts of the case.
I should like hon. gentlemen to pay attention to this letter, which will enable them to form an opinion as to where we are at in connection with this treaty.
We might state that we protested against the ratification of the Australian treaty before there was any announcement of the impending election, and politics therefore had nothing whatever to do with our statement. The danger of injury to the dairy interests in western Canada resulting from the Australian treaty is real. As you probably know, New Zealand, which is the largest exporter of butter in the world, automatically benefits from the lowering in duty. Both of these countries are in a position to land butter for sale in Vancouver during our winter at a much lower price per pound, consequently they will govern the market, whether or not they land a pound of butter in Canada. They may not import much butter into Canada, but they will govern the price, as Canada will have to meet their quotations to keep their butter out.
The farmer of western Canada who produces the cream will be obliged to assume the burden in the form of lower prices for butter fat. This in a few words is the situation. Just how serious this loss will be only future experience can say.
And yet we are told by the Minister of Agriculture that world prices are regulated by supply and demand. When I quote the words of one who has been following this industry-and no industry has ever received 14011-55J
closer attention at the hands of any organization than has this industry at the hands of P. Bums & Company-I think the House will be inclined to aocept the statements contained in the letter regarding the probable disastrous effects of the Australian treaty upon our dairy industry. May I also state in this connection that of the first shipment of butter that came in from Australia, we find P. Burns & Company one of the largest purchasers. Why? Because he has endeavoured to control the trade of western Canada, and in order to do that he found it necessary to handle the butter shipped in from New Zealand and Australia so that they could obtain the product of these other countries to compete against the trade which he has maintained for a great number of years.

Does the hon. gentleman think that it is in the interests of western Canada, or of Canada as a whole, to have the control of the price of butter in the hands of cold storage people, such as Pat Burns?

I do not know whether the cold storage methods have much bearing upon the market values or not, but I do know that the cold storage methods are a great asset to the producers of butter and other farm products, and if it were not for our cold storage system throughout the Dominion many of our products could not be sent to market. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) told us a little while ago that we in the Dominion of Canada produced 275,000,000 pounds of butter per year. I think if the hon. minister looks up the statistics which come from his own department, he will find that he is about 100,000,000 pounds out; that the production of the Dominion of Canada last year was approximately 195,000,000, instead of 275,000,000 as stated by the minister.

I was including
both dairy and creamery butter.
How did the minister arrive at the figures?
The memorandum was prepared by one of my officers.

I can easily understand the department being able to arrive at figures in connection with butter that comes through a factory, but as to the butter produced on the farm and consumed on the farm, it is almost impossible to get the figures.
Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) told us that we had a saving clause in that agreement, and we are all glad we
86S
The Address-Mr. Davis

have it. That saving clause is.the provision for the annulment of the treaty, and that is the only thing that can save us. I suggest to the farmer representatives in this House that irrespective of the occupation in which we engage, we should have not only the dairy interests but every other interest affecting this country at heart. However, the question now before the House is one that deals with dairy and fruit interests in particular.
Reference has been made to the importation of butter, and the statistics have been given in this House. I hold in my hand information to the effect that there has been shipped into the Dominion of Canada since this treaty came into effect 3,727,174 pounds of butter.
What authority?

The information which I have here, I will go so far as to say, is considerably more authentic than that which the minister says he has received. I have before me a letter addressed to the Central Creameries Limited, dated November 14th, 1925, with regard to a quantity of butter arriving at Vancouver from New Zealand. I need not go into that, however, because the details have already been given in this debate. But let me read the following letter dated January 18, 1926, addressed to myself.
Received your wire reading:
"Wire giving all particulars re shipments of Australian and New Zealand butter since November fourteenth."
Immediately upon receipt of same, I replied as follows :
"January seventh 11,768 fifty-six pound boxes arrived Vancouver distributed as follows: 1,000 boxes for Victoria, 6,000 for eastern Canada and 4,768 for Vancouver Writing," which I beg to confirm.
I further wish to mention that of the 4,768 boxes for Vancouver, there wore 320 boxes consigned to the orient, leaving a total of 4,448 booxes for Vancouver distributors.
This is absolutely correct information and I am sorry to say that there is more butter on the way both for eastern and western Canada, but I do not know how much.
As already stated, this butter arrived on January 7th at Vancouver, and on January 11th the butter-fat prices in Alberta were reduced two cents per pound to the producers, and the butter prices, wholesale and retail, both in Alberta and British Columbia, were reduced three cents per pound. In other words, the Australian treaty will simply reduce the price of butter-fat, not alone in Alberta and British Columbia, but in the whole of the Dominion of Canada from the time of the arrival of the butter from the antipodes, and as long as any of those goods are on our market. Such are the actual conditions.
Any information which I can give you on this or any other subject, I shall be glad to furnish.
Then, following that was a telegram to the effect that 3,000,000 pounds were in transit. Following that telegram is a statement from
Mr. Davis J	- .
Henderson-Stuart, Limited, of Winnipeg, who are, I understand, brokers for New Zealand and Australia butter merchants, which reads as follows:
There are some 3,000,000 pounds New Zealands and Australians arriving at Atlantic and Pacific ports between now and February 6th, and more following. Most dealers in the east, and no doubt in the far west, were buyers, and pending arrival of their purchases, the weakness on spot butters is, not surprisingly somewhat aggravated. Past. Firsts at 40 cents is the nominal outside price on local sales.
In dealing with that question the Minister of Finance last night in his remarks made a statement which to me was a very convincing fact, as to the absolute necessity of maintaining our home market for our home product. When the Minister of Finance made the statement last night that there was a large quantity 'of Canadian butter shipped to England, and when that Canadian butter came in contact with! New Zealand and Australian butter, the unsold portion of the consignment was brought back to this country rather than sold at a sacrifice on the British market. That consignment consisted of 8,000 boxes, approxi mately 448,000 poundte. I do not think we car ask for any better evidence of the necessitj of a home market for home production. When we in Canada find it necessary to recall a large shipment of butter made to a European market, it is a matter of no small significance. What we do say is that so long as the dairy industry of this Dominion can produce sufficient butter for the requirements of the people of this country, this market should be retained for our own producers.
I have devoted a few minutes to the dairy interests, and I want now to take up the Australian treaty as a whole. While the dairy interests in this country are vitally affected by the treaty, we have other interests in this Canada of ours that are going to be affected to an even more serious extent by this treaty.
The first items I find referred to in the treaty are fresh beef, pork, mutton and lamb When you realize that we can scarcely find a market for these products that we raise in this country, and that our trade relations are such that Canada imported of these products last year the tremendous amount of 9,363,093 pounds, I say that instead of reducing our tariff upon these commodities that compete with our own industries, the duty should have been raised to a higher level than before. The duty upon these products was reduced under the treaty from two cents to one-half a cent a pound, and if you apply that reduction to the amount of these products that came into the Dominion during the year ended March 31, 1925, it would mean a loss to the treasury of $140,446.36.


The Address-Mr. Davis
On canned meats, poultry, game, and extracts of meats this government saw fit to reduce the duty from 17i to 15 per cent. Up to the Gist March, 1925, we imported of these products 1,485,876 pounds, and the reduction in duty on that amount would mean a loss to the treasury of this country of $37,146.90.
On lard and lard compounds the duty is reduced by the treaty li cents per pound. That was the former duty; now these products come in free. This reduction of 11 cents per pound in the duty has been made to enable the producers of lard in Australia and New Zealand to compete with this great industry we have here in this Dominion. Last year we imported 6,138,558 pounds, and the reduction in the duty on that amount imported would mean a loss to the treasury of $92,078.37.
On beeswax the duty was formerly 5 per cent; now beeswax comes in free. Last year we imported 149,273 pounds; the reduction in duty on that amount would mean a loss to the treasury of $2,572.
On eggs there was formerly a duty of two cents a dozen; eggs now come in free under the treaty. While I am free to admit that at the present time there may not be any New Zealand or Australian eggs imported into Canada, this concession in the treaty is so great as to induce them to educate their people, just as we have done in this country, to increase their egg production so that they can take advantage of this market which is offered them under the treaty. We imported last year 2,695,047 dozen of eggs, which would mean with the reduction in duty a loss to the treasury of $53,900.94.
On cheese, the government saw fit to remove the duty of two cents a pound altogether; cheese now comes in free. In the year 1925 -I am taking the statistics of the Department of Agriculture, which do not agree with the figures given by the Minister of Agriculture -we imported 4,544,485 pounds of cheese, with the reduction in duty that would mean a loss to the treasury of $90,889.70.
There are several other items which 1 shall not take up, but I want to'deal with canned vegetables.

I think I hoard the hon. member say that we imported 4,000,000
pounds of cheese. Were those figures obtained from the Customs department?

No, from the minister's own
department.
I explained that.

Oh, no. The figures I am
giving were importations for the year ending March 31, 1925.
Mr.- MOTHERWELL:	That was before
the treaty.

Absolutely, but does the
minister mean to tell the House that the government's own statistics are incorrect?
No.
The figures I have given are the government's own figures.

They were put
there for an entirely different purpose-as a basis for the collection of duties.

Being government statistics
I take it they are correct.
The duty on canned vegetables was formerly one cent a pound; under the treaty they come in free. Last year we imported 13,608,542 pounds of canned vegetables, which with the reduction in duty would mean a loss to the treasury of $136,085.42.
Now I come to canned fruits. One could scarcely conceive, in view of present conditions in the fruit industry both in the east and the west, that any further encouragement would be given to outside producers to compete in our own market. Of canned fruits we imported last year 15,253,675 pounds, and upon that there was a duty of If cents per pound. Under the treaty the duty is now one-half a cent a pound, which would mean a loss to the treasury of $190,680.94, and at the same time enable the producers of canned fruits in other countries to come into competition with our own producers at home. But the most important thing in connection with fruit is the reductions that have been made in the duty on fruit pulp. Mr. Speaker. I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION IN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION IN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext: I want to inquire of the leader of the House whether the government has any information as to the intention of the British Ministry of Pensions or of the Imperial government to take over the administration of imperial pensions in Canada and the United States, which administration has been carried on for some years by the Canadian government for the imperial authorities. Also, whether the government has notice of any claim in regard to maladministration, or overcharge, or excessive payments in connection with these pensions, and, if so, what amount is involved.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Leader of the House):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION IN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext: I will make the necessary inquiries. I am unable to answer my hon. friend offhand but I shall give him the information as soon as I obtain it.
On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to bring to the attention of the government, and particularly of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), a telegram which I have received1 from the President of the Women's Canadian Club of Fort William with reference to an American magazine which has published certain undesirable literature in relation to the late Queen Alexandra. I shall not mention the name of the magazine in question, as I have no desire to give it a free advertisement; I will communicate the name privately to the minister. The telegram reads:
We are greatly shocked and indignant at articles now appearing on the life of Her Majesty the late Queen Alexandra in magazine dates February 6 and 13. Is there any law against objectionable printed matter that could prevent the sale in Canada of the magazine or is there any department of the government that could investigate and keep out these truly vile articles?
This telegram is signed by Mrs. John Dyke, President of the Women's Canadian Club of Fort William. I know this lady very well and have a high regard for her, and I have no doubt- whatever that the articles are as described. In the circumstances I think the government should do something to stop the circulation of such literature in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Leader of the House):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am obliged to my hon. friend for giving me the name of the magazine. I will 
communicate immediately with the Postmaster General, who has charge of such matters, and will let the hon. member know the result later.

I may observe that a
good deal of this literature comes in by freight or express and not through the post office.
On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Mr. L. W. JOHNSTONE (Cape Breton North-Victoria):
speechtext:
Mfay I ask the government a question in view of a telegram which I have received- from Sydney from the Hon. Senator McCormick? The telegram, which speaks for itself, reads:
On receipt of vour message yesterday I telegraphed McLurg and have just received his night letter reply which reads: Sydney, February 8, 1920, Hon. John McCormick, Senator, Answering your telegram no arrangement has been made with C.N.R. for sale Princess coal. Canadian National offered to accept 15,000 tons of screened Princess coal to apply on the option they gave us to bank 120,000 tons Dominion coal. The directors of the N.S. Steel and Coal Co., decided they were unable to accept offer to bank 15,000 tons Princess which to provide relief would give Princess mine two days' work per week for six or seven weeks for the reason that the loss to the company would be too great. We understood Dr. Johnstone, M.P., was endeavouring secure rail freight rate on Princess coal to Quebec and Montreal which would enable us to sell and ship Princess coal by rail. Signed J. E. McLurg. Surely the Alberta rate for 25,000 tons to Ontario should apply to this small order in our desperate situation.
It appears from this telegram that no relief has so far been afforded the miners of northern Cape Breton-
Order.

-and I wish to ask if the government has made any effort to secure the same rate for the transportation of coal pro rata from points in Nova Scotia to central Canada as now applies to the transportation of coal from Alberta. This appears to be the only way to relieve the present destitution at Sydney Mines.
Order.

I would remind the House that lengthy questions such as that which the hon. member is now putting to the government should form the subject of a notice. The Speaker invariably allows some latitude in the asking of questions on the orders of the day, but such questions should not be of a complex nature.

As I apprehend the privilege, questions on the orders of the day, while not unlimited, are certainly not so

Questions on Order Paper
limited as to exclude inquiries on the answer to which depends the immediate livelihood of vast masses of people. Surely they are within the rule of urgency. It is true the telegram is rather long, but the question is short and simple. I may point out also, Mr. Speaker, that if the question goes on the order paper it means there will be no answer for six weeks. What is to become of the men in the meantime?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Mines, and as I am very much interested in this matter as representing a Nova Scotia riding, I will call his attention to the question of my hon. friend, and I have no doubt my colleague will see that he gets an answer.

I would refer the House to the usage as regards the putting of questions on the orders of the day, which will be found in'paragraph 311 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, and in Bourinot at pages 364 and 365:
When the orders of the day are called by the Speaker and before they are read by the Clerk Assistant, it is the practice sanctioned by usage but not by any positive rule, for members to make personal explanations or ask questions of the government, in reference to an inaccurate report of their speeches in the official

charges made against them in the public prints; or in reference to certain remarks which had been misunderstood on a previous occasion, and which they had not before had an opportunity of explaining; or in respect to delay in obtaining returns or to the incompleteness of certain returns brought down under the order of the House; or relative to the state of public business, or other matters of public interest. But these remarks should be brief as they are only tolerated, these being no question before the Chair when they are made, and no discussion should be allowed when a minister has replied to a question nor after a member has made his personal explanation. In asking a question, a member must not attack the conduct of the government. If a member wishes to make personal explanations in reference to remarks which have fallen from another member, the latter ought to be in his place.
Although the matter has already been debated at considerable length in the House, I realize that it is of great importance. However, the question in regard to it should be brief and to the point; and when it is of a complex nature, as this seems to be, notice should be given. At all events, I am quite sure that the members of the government who have listened to the rather involved question put by the hon. member will see that it is answered to-morrow.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) if it is the intention of the government to grant on 15,000 tons of coal from Cape Breton to Montreal the same
pro rata mileage rate as he said he was willing to grant for the transportation of 25,000 tons of coal from Alberta to Ontario?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (West Edmonton, Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would remind my hon. friend that the government of Canada does not fix railway rates. The freight rates on the Canadian National Railways are under the control of their board of management. They have the privilege, if they desire, of fixing a rate on the movement from Nova Scotia commensurate with the rate fixed on the other movement, from Alberta to Ontario. I wish to make it very clear that neither the federal government nor any of its ministers had anything to do with the fixing of the rate from Alberta to Ontario.

May I ask the hon. gentleman another question? Is it true that he stated in his place a few days ago that he had arranged for 25,000 tons of Alberta coal to be moved to Toronto at the current rate of $7 a ton? Also, will he make a statement with regard to the 15,000 tons of coal from Cape Breton?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that, Mr. Speaker. I have been very careful in my answers in this House to make it absolutely clear that the government has nothing to do with the fixing of freight rates. The government is willing to use its good offices in an effort to alleviate any distress in our coal-mining districts. Let me say distinctly, as I said before, that the government had nothing whatever to do with the fixing of the rate referred to. The granting of such a rate is the prerogative of the railway company.

Mr. Speaker,, the matter of questions has been referred to, I would remind the House that we have a rule which makes the debate on the Address continuous. I do not see why that rule should be perpetuated, because the questions that are put on the order paper ought to get immediate attention, although in fact usually it is several weeks before they are dealt with. I would draw the attention of the committee on rules to the desirability of revising the rule in this respect so that questions on the order paper may be answered every day in the ordinary way.

speechtext:
A committee sat last
year for the purpose of revising the rules of the House.
Proposed Legislation

do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

It is unfortunate that
the report of this committee was not adopted last session, for in that event the extended debate on the Address that is now proceeding would have been curtailed long ago.

subtopic: REFERENCES TO CANADA IN BRITISH PRESS

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: REFERENCES TO CANADA IN BRITISH PRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted
to call the attention of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization to a Canadian Press cable report of a speech made by the newly appointed Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia, Mr. Bruce, in London last night, in which he deprecates attacks made on Canada by some British newspapers, and says:
It peeved one to come home to see malicious articles with reference to Canada, not only in the rags of the Old Country press, but in reputable journals.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I too read the press despatch this morning to which my hon. friend refers. Up to the present I have not had my attention called to articles of this kind appearing in the British press, but I have been advised that some speeches made in this House on certain occasions have been reproduced in the English papers. I doubt whether we can take any action to prohibit that being done. The House resumed from Tuesday, February 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. C. Elliott for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Sutherland (South Oxford).

Mr. Speaker, when I moved the adjournment of the debate last night I was dealing with the reductions made by the Australian treaty in the duties on farm products. The next item with which I wish to deal is honey. The duty on honey was reduced by the treaty from two cents to one cent a pound. We imported 108,809 pounds of honey last year, valued at S19,205. Fruit pulp, not sweetened, which formerly carried a duty of 17 per cent, is now

The Address-Mr. Davis
admitted free. The duty on tallow, which was formerly 17i per cent, was reduced to 10 per cent. On dried apples and evaporated fruits the duty was reduced from 17J to 10 per cent. Taking into consideration the total imports for the one year prior to March 31, 1925, the reductions in duty made by the Australian treaty would mean a loss to the treasury of the Dominion of Canada of no less a sum than $772,826.
Yesterday I referred to certain shipments of butter from Australia and New Zealand. I find that on November 14, 1925, 1,200 packages of butter, amounting to 67,200 pounds arrived from New Zealand and Australia. On January 7, 1926, there were imported 11,768 packages, 56 pounds to the package, or a total of 659,974 pounds. There have arrived within the last few days or are now in transit a further 3,000,000 pounds. In all during a period of three months under this treaty we have imported into Canada from Australia and New Zealand, 3,727,174 pounds of butter, while for the year preceding March 31, 1925, we imported only 198,341 pounds; showing that since the introduction of this treaty there has been an increased importation into the Dominion of Canada in a period of three months as compared with the year previous, of 3,528,833 pounds.
Another very important commodity in which consideration is given to the Australians in this treaty is mutton. I well remember the day, Mr. Speaker, when out in the western provinces it was almost impossible to find a market for our western mutton. I well remember the day when mutton from Australia came into Vancouver ports in shipload lots. Finally measures were taken for the purpose of preventing the shipment of mutton from Australia to Canada, and from that day to this the sheep industry in Canada has improved as time progressed, to such an extent that it is now one of the most important and profitable industries we have in the western provinces. Under the treaty I find the duty on mutton has been reduced from two cents a pound to one-half cent a pound. That is simply opening up the market again for shipments of mutton from Australia, and I fear it will have the effect of producing the conditions we had in days gone by, of practically destroying the sheep industry in the western provinces. I will assume the responsibility of saying that in my opinion, while we have four million sheep in Canada to-day, the introduction of this treaty means a loss to the owners of sheep of at least $2 per head. If, as is stated in the letter which was read to the House yesterday from P. Burns & Company, of Calgary,
referring to the effect the lowering of the duty on butter will have in Canada, it matters not whether any butter comes in from Australia or not, our market will be affected just the same-and that is the general opinion, Mr. Speaker, of those interested in this great and growing butter industry-the reduction in duty on butter alone means a loss to the butter producers of Canada, on their production of 190,000,000 pounds last year, of $3,800,000. The reduction in the duty on cheese, which is also a product of butter fat, will mean a loss to our producers, on their production last year of 175,000,000 pounds, of $3,400,000. I submit, therefore, to this House that there is very great danger of the destruction of one of the most important industries we have in the Dominion of Canada, an industry which both Dominion and provincial governments have spent enormous sums of money to help build up and improve. I congratulate federal governments of the past upon their efforts in that direction; I congratulate our provincial governments for spending the money they have in endeavouring to build up different lines in connection with farming, ranching and the fruit industry of this Dominion; but I regret very, very much that we had introduced during the last session legislation which I fear will retard much of the progress we have made in the past.
I find that after the Australian treaty was adopted in this House, an order in council was passed by this government granting certain concessions to New Zealand. In order to get our products into New Zealand we have to pay upon lard for instance a duty of 20 per cent ad valorem, while their lard can be shipped into Canada free of duty. On milk and milk products including butter and cheese, we are compelled to pay a duty of 25 per cent when we ship our products to New Zealand, while their products of a similar nature come in here under a duty of one cent a pound. We pay 3^ cents a pound on fish going to New Zealand, while their fish comes in here under the treaty. On fruit pulp we pay a duty of 3 cents a pound going to New Zealand, while their fruit pulp comes in here free. On meat we pay 20 per cent going to New Zealand, while they are able to ship their meats into Canada under a duty of one-half cent a pound.
I should like to deal with this order in council, because I think it gives us a little information which we had no conception of up to a short time ago. The order in council passed by this government is No. 1757, is dated Government House, Ottawa, September 26, 1925, and reads:
The Address-Mr. Davis

The Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General m Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, is pleased to order that under the provisions of section 5 of the Australian Trade Agreement Act, 1925, and subject to the provisions of said act, the rates of duties set out in Schedule 2 of the same act shall be and the same are hereby extended to goods the produce or manufacture of New Zealand when imported into Canada.
Yesterday the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) the following question as reported on page 864 of Hansard:
Mr. Sutherland (South Oxford):	My hon. friend
invited questions before he sat down. What concessions were received from New Zealand by extending to that country the same treaty that was extended to Australia, and what pressure was brought to bear by New Zealand to secure the advantages Australia had received?
The Minister of Agriculture gave this intelligent answer:
Mr. Motherwell:	I will answer that very shortly.
I do not know all the details, but I know that we are all in the one family.
I thought my hon. friend* knew some of the details.

According to the order that has been passed in council, we as a Canadian people do not enjoy the same privileges and rights in connection with this treaty as we do in connection with the treaty with Australia. The order in council provides that our markets can be used for the shipment of Australian products for which we receive no consideration whatever. Therefore I say that if we have a government which is willing to open up our markets, under conditions which this order in council provides, for the products of other countries in competition with our own products without receiving any consideration whatever, it is the duty of this parliament to deal with the situation. If any minister to-day is of the opinion that I have made in this House an assertion that is not correct, I will give him a few moments to take an opportunity of correcting it.
Under this treaty the fruit industry of the Dominion of Canada is threatened to a very great extent. While last year we did not import any fruit pulp, so far as I can gather, the duty on fruit pulp was reduced from 17i per cent to nothing. What was the result? I have in my hand a memorandum of the statement made by the Premier of Australia. He said:
Will Send To Canada Trade Representative.
Melbourne, Australia, February 5.-Premier Stanley M. Bruce announced in tlie House of Representatives to-day that efforts were being made by the govern-

ment to arrange with the dried fruits industry and other business interests for the appointment of a trade representative in Canada. The government, he added, was also considering making similar appointments in South Africa and elsewhere.
That in itself is something for us to consider. If the Australian government are of opinion that, under this treaty which they have entered into with us, they can protect the growers of fruit, the manufacturers of fruit pulp, 'by exploiting the markets of the Dominion of Canada at the expense of our own fruit producers, I ask the House to consider this matter and to record its vote in favour of the amendment so as to protect that industry. I find on looking through Hansard of a year ago that the Australian treaty met with some opposition amongst our Progressive friends, but some of them, representing as they did the farming industry, not only voted for the Australian treaty but spoke in favour of it. What is the result? There is not one man sitting at that end of the House to-day who recorded his vote in favour of the Australian treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend has read
very carefully the debates of last session, will he tell us how many Conservatives supported the Australian treaty and asked us to put it through?

I am not familiar with how
many did so, but those Conservatives are here; just as other hon. members are here to answer for the votes which they recorded. Three or four on this side of the House may have supported that treaty, but a government that attempts to justify its position or its actions by referring to what others have done, is not worthy of the confidence of the people. In that little group down at the end of the chamber which last year consisted of some sixty representatives of farming and agriculture, we do not find one who recorded his vote in favour of that treaty. But we do find at the head of that group an hon. gentleman who voiced his opposition to it, who shirked his vote on that occasion; and I adk that hon. gentleman to explain to this House the reason why he did not give the organization which he represents that interest and support which it rightly deserves.
I want to deal for a few moments with the importance of the industry of which I am speaking. I do not wish any hon. member to think my mind runs in the direction of the protection of only one particular industry. But we have another class of farmers without any assets whatever, and that is the farmer that farms the farmer. In the organization to which I belong, namely, the United Farmers of Alberta, many of the conventions and meetings of which I have attended, we have a great deal of community singing, and it is usually very effective. I am going to read one of the favourite songs for the benefit of the House, a song which will apply to no occasion more aptly than it does at the present time. It was adopted as an official campaign song by the United Farmers of Alberta at their annual convention in 1920.
